0.title: Course Introduction
0.content:
In the whole Loire Valley, two tiny sweet-wine regions are recognised as among France's greatest sweet whites, comparable to Sauternes and Alsace SGN: Quarts-de-Chaume Grand Cru and Bonnezeaux. Both have Chenin Blanc and noble rot (Botrytis) as their soul, planted on the schist slopes of the Layon valley, yet each shows a very different great personality because of its own distinctive plots.

Learning Objectives

🍯 Get to know Quarts-de-Chaume Grand Cru in depth

The Loire Valley's only Grand Cru-level AOC (passed in 2011), a miniature region of about 40 hectares

🌺 Understand Bonnezeaux's distinctive terroir

Also on the Layon schist slopes, but Bonnezeaux is larger and more exuberant in personality

🌫️ Grasp how noble rot (Botrytis) works

How the Layon valley's special morning mist lets noble rot develop to create top sweet wines
1.title: The Layon Valley: A Natural Cradle for Sweet Wines
1.highlights.0.title: Morning mist
1.highlights.0.content: Every autumn the Layon valley's morning mist provides a damp environment for Botrytis cinerea (grey mould), letting noble rot develop on the grape skin as water evaporates and sugar, acidity and aroma all concentrate
1.highlights.1.title: Dry afternoons
1.highlights.1.content: The key is the alternating cycle of "misty damp + sunny dry" — afternoon sun dries the grape skins, preventing the mould from spreading excessively and ensuring it is beneficial "noble rot" rather than harmful "grey rot"
1.highlights.2.title: Schist slopes
1.highlights.2.content: The Layon valley's south-facing schist (schiste) slopes retain heat well and reflect sunlight, helping the grapes ripen fully, while the schist's mineral character gives the sweet wines a distinctive salty minerality
1.content:
The Layon is a southern tributary of the Loire, and its valley provides one of France's most perfect terroir settings for sweet wine. The valley is not wide, but its distinctive microclimate gathers several top sweet-wine AOCs: Coteaux-du-Layon, Coteaux-du-Layon Villages, and the two jewels in the crown — Bonnezeaux and Quarts-de-Chaume.

🔬 The science of noble rot (Botrytis cinerea)

Grey mould exists in two forms, "beneficial (noble rot)" and "harmful (grey rot)." The process of proper noble-rot infection:

  1. Morning mist supplies humidity and the hyphae enter the grape skin (but the grape remains intact and does not rot)
  2. Afternoon sun dries and evaporates water, and the skin shrivels ("rôti" = as if roasted)
  3. Sugar concentrates from 20% to 30–40%, Chenin's high acidity still supports the sweetness, and the special "noble-rot aromas" (honey, ginger, orange peel, dried apricot) form

3.title: Quarts-de-Chaume Grand Cru — The Loire's Summit
3.content:
Quarts-de-Chaume (AOC established in 1954, Grand Cru status formally recognised by regulation in 2011, applicable from the 2010 vintage) is the smallest and most precious sweet-wine region in the Loire Valley.

📐 Area: about 40 hectares

It is so rare because the law allows only wines made on these roughly 40 hectares of specific slopes to use the name; producers can be counted on one hand, and total production is tiny.

🪨 Geology: quartzite + schist

Quarts-de-Chaume lies in the village of Rochefort-sur-Loire, with soils mainly of quartzite and schist (slightly different from Bonnezeaux's schist), giving more mineral depth and a tighter structure.

📜 History: the origin of "Quarts"

"Quarts" means "quarter" — in the Middle Ages this vineyard was managed by the abbey (Abbaye de Ronceray), and a quarter of each year's harvest had to be handed to the lord. This share was called "la quart" and gradually evolved into the place name.

🍷 Style characteristics

Young (1–5 years): golden colour; honey, fresh apricot, white peach, acacia blossom and the fresh sweetness of ginger, with acidity as high as pH 3.2 perfectly balancing the sweetness

Aged (10–30 years): deep golden-brown, with a complex evolution of candied orange peel, ginger sugar, toasted coconut, toffee, roasted hazelnut and smoky minerality, known as the "rancio" character, one of the Loire's most mysterious ageing transformations

Representative estates: Domaine des Baumard, Château Pierre-Bise, Château de Bellerive
4.title: Bonnezeaux — A More Exuberant Poem of Sweet Wine
4.content:
Bonnezeaux AOC (1951) lies in the village of Thouarcé, about 92 hectares (nearly three times larger than Quarts-de-Chaume), yet it is still one of France's smallest and rarest AOCs. It sits in the same Layon tributary system as Quarts-de-Chaume, but its style is more exuberant and rich.

🪨 Soil differences

Bonnezeaux's three main slopes (La Montagne, Beauregard, Fesles) are mainly deep purple schist (schiste violet), which retains heat better than Quarts-de-Chaume's quartzite, making wines with deeper colour and richer, more exuberant aromas.

5.title: Quick Quiz
5.questions.0.question: Where does the "Quarts" in Quarts-de-Chaume come from?
5.questions.0.options.0: French for "seasons," meaning grapes can be harvested all year
5.questions.0.options.1: In the medieval abbey era, the quarter of the vineyard's harvest owed to the lord
5.questions.0.options.2: French for "quartz," referring to the abundant quartzite in the soil
5.questions.0.explanation: "Quarts" refers to a "quarter (quart)" — in the Middle Ages this vineyard was managed by the abbey, and a quarter of each year's harvest had to be handed to the lord. This share ("la quart") gradually became the place name and evolved into today's Quarts-de-Chaume.
5.questions.1.question: What key natural conditions do Layon valley sweet wines depend on?
5.questions.1.options.0: Strong sunshine from a Mediterranean climate
5.questions.1.options.1: An alternating cycle of morning mist (encouraging noble rot) + afternoon sun (drying the grape skins)
5.questions.1.options.2: Abundant groundwater, keeping the vines safe from drought
5.questions.1.explanation: Noble-rot sweet wines need a precise alternation of "wet" and "dry": the Layon valley's morning mist provides the humidity for noble rot to infect the grapes, while afternoon sun dries the skins and prevents harmful grey rot. This microclimate cycle is the key to making top sweet wines.
5.questions.2.question: What is the main stylistic difference between Bonnezeaux and Quarts-de-Chaume?
5.questions.2.options.0: Bonnezeaux uses Sauvignon Blanc, Quarts-de-Chaume uses Chenin Blanc
5.questions.2.options.1: Quarts-de-Chaume is more refined and mineral; Bonnezeaux is richer and more exuberant, with more obvious tropical fruit
5.questions.2.options.2: The styles are exactly the same, differing only in area
5.questions.2.options.3: Bonnezeaux is a dry white, only Quarts-de-Chaume is sweet
5.questions.2.explanation: Both have Chenin Blanc and noble rot at their core, but soil differences create a clear stylistic split: Quarts-de-Chaume (quartzite) is more refined and mineral; Bonnezeaux (deep purple schist, which retains more heat) is richer and more exuberant, with tropical honey and mango aromas more prominent.
